Jan,1998   No.125   Page Reply

 How to write to us...02     -

 Vic Bishop...........03    10

 Sintech..............13     -

 Miles Kinloch........15    25

 A.P. Blatherwick.....26    27

 Grahame Parkyn.......28    30

 L.G. Baumann.........31    38

   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From: Vic Bishop, LANCS






Dear Brian,

I have had a good look at OUTLET
123 and read the comments by
Bernadette Dowsland and yourself
which to me (as a seldom contri-
buting but very interested subs-
criber) suggests that there is a
great danger of Spectrum losing
out to PC. I for one would be
more than a little upset by this
as I personally find the subscr-
iption cost to be very good val-
ue.


I do not intend to compare OUT-
LET with ALCHNEWS; they are
complementary - not competitive
and both have their strengths
and weaknesses. "You can please
some of the people some of the
time etc". However I do think
there is a case for Bi-monthly
in which instance you might feel
it possible to show some reduct-
ion in the price?.

I am not at all sure that most
us know what we want from our
computers (I use the embracing
term). I know that many subscri-
bers have switched from Spectrum
to PC, I have thought about it
but to date cannot see any real
benefit to me. Who can tell me
that I am wrong?


I would like to follow on from
Bernadette who I praise for be-
ing prepared to be forthright, I
allow for the fact that it's un-
usual for someone from Yorkshire
and she makes a lot of sense (do
not have a go at me Bernadette,
I'm not a Lancastrian) I suggest
that we all need to think about
where we are going. What about a
full discussion on the merits of
Spectrum against PC and vice
versa.

I will try and provoke by saying
(quite seriously) that I have a
Spectrum 128+2 Grey(but with the
ROM from the 128 Black with the
heat sink which includes tape
tester and one or two other adv-
antages) a double disc drive(2),


a CUB Microvitec 653 monitor
which includes sound, a Citizen
120 printer with a P16 interface
from which I can get emphasised
(better than NLC) print, large
and extra large print (without
having to use codes) Apart from
hoping to get a 24 dot printer
at the right price I am fairly
satisfied with what it will do.


I cannot understand why people
still use 48's 48+ other 128's
Microdrives ZX and Alphacom
printers and cassette tapes.
They were good in their day but
using them now seems like an
incentive to go over to PC -
possibly the wrong decision?.


I feel that I have the best
possible Spectrum set up. What
do CHEZRON, Malcom Perry and
other names recommend and why?

Now to Software: I am not inter-
ested in games other than Golf
and such like. I have Tasword
and Tasword plus 2 which looks
after all my correspondence etc.
I have Masterfile, Wordmaster
and most of the instructive
software and thanks to Outlet
and Alchnews programmes such as
Wipeout, Transit and Clone-it. I
have plenty of educational prog-
rams (French, Biology, Maths,
computer studies and of course
machine code etc). I don't use
them all the time but have sess-
ions like most people.


I've an excellent comprehensive
program for stocks and shares
and can get full print outs. I
would like to spend more time on
graphics and programming but
struggle with them - I feel sure
plenty of other subscribers find
as I do that it's hard to do it
on your own with no-one close at
hand that you can work out prob-
lems with. PLEASE:- NO suggest-
ions such as founding a Speccy
commune, or finding someone with
a Spectrum that would be prepar-
ed to have someone like me liv-
ing next door to them.

What about the possibility of
some tutorials with help sect-
ions or even tests with answers
in the next edition?


I know that 30 hour Basic sets
out to cover this but some of
the examples have slight errors
and I find a great many of the
explanations difficult to under-
stand which all adds up to a
disincentive!. I wonder how many
people have not used their Spec-
trum very much and have then
switched to a PC and are not us-
ing that very much either?.

Others I am sure will have very
different ideas about their
requirements, I hope you get
plenty of correspondence on the
subject and look forward to you
own comments. Please do all you
can to keep Spectrum healthy.

          V.R. Bishop

Brian Cavers to Vic Bishop

We are giving a lot of thought
at this time to the future of
OUTLET and welcome comments,Vic.

OUTCLASS was set up to be a tut-
orial,primarily for programming,
but these days depends more and
more on readers' contributing
articles as I have less and less
time available! (the usual
whinge).

As far as hardware, I cannot get
along with 128K BASIC - I think
it is dreadful. I know that a
128K machine includes 48K BASIC
but I have a +3 with 128K and an
emulator on the PC so have no
need to change my main 48K!


I also touchtype (yes touchtype
in Spectrum 48K BASIC!) and use
the excellent Fuller keyboard
for this purpose. The +3 key-
board (which I think is the same
for the other 128Ks is almost
useless for touchtyping.I'm sure
it is possible to do so but as
the keyboard is non-standard
(for instance, the right little
finger rests on the ENTER key!)
then if you got used to it then
normal keyboards would become
difficult (it's bad enough as it
is with the variations in the
positions of #, `, " and so on
between Spectrum, SAM and PC!)

I use a fast Epson dot-matrix
printer which meets my needs and
is shared via a switch between
three computers.

I find the +D excellent - the
only problem I get is edge-conn-
ector fluctuations which is more
the fault of the Spectrum than
the +D. I keep meaning to try
silver or gold paint to improve
it but have never got round to
it.

+D DOS seems faster than the PC
when using a floppy disk. The PC
seems to stop and think about it
whenever it looks at a floppy
disk whereas the +D just rapidly
goes ahead!
                      Brian

From:       SINTECH,
    Gastackerstr. 23, 70794
     Filderstadt, Germany,

Dear Ron,

I read in OUTLET that some of
the readers have had problems in
connecting a PSU to their
drives. Well, using a +2A/+3 PSU
is a good and cheap possibility,
but for those who don't want to
solder new connectors, we have a
solution...


We have invented the POWERKIT,
which is nothing else than a
small plug, exchanging the plug
which normally supplies the
Spectrum +2 A/+3 to 3 plugs: 2
for two 3,5" drives and one with
an extra 5V supply, as some
interfaces might need it (MB02+
for example). This powerkit is
available for 5,00 P + 2,00 P
postage from the above address.

            Thomas

From: Miles Kinloch, EDINBURGH


Dear Brian,

Sorry it's been so long since
I've been in touch, but my spare
time has been limited as I've
been at college. However, here
are a couple of snippets I
thought may be of interest to
your readers.

When experimenting recently with
the Betados facility to create
extended directory formats, I
discovered that things go wrong
when the file capacity specified
exceeds 255, affecting the cata-
logue display and file position
referencing.


I traced the cause to the fact
that the DOS uses a single-byte
system variable (at location
15874) for the directory slot
number which, although adequate
for the 80-file format for which
it was designed, can only cope
with a maximum possible value of
255. Since to substitute a
two-byte system variable would
involve extensive reprogramming
of the DOS,and since a practical
limit of 240 files (the nearest
value corresponding to a compl-
ete set of directory tracks)
still offers a generous capacity
the easiest way may be just to
accept these constraints and
POKE the DOS to restrict the
range of the FORMAT parameter.


To recap, the maximum number of
directory tracks is presently
39, representing 780 files. A
disk would be formatted in this
way using FORMAT d1,n where 'n'
is the number of directory
tracks in the format, in this
case 39. With any higher number,
an 'Integer out of range' error
would occur. To set a maximum
size of 240 files, then, we
would want to reduce the highest
permitted value for 'n' to 12,
and this can be achieved by
altering the DOS as follows:-

10 CLEAR 4e4
20 LOAD d1"+sys Beta"CODE 40960
30 POKE 46415,9
40 SAVE d1"+sys Beta"CODE 40960,
   6850


(From the point of view of
BETAFIX, it makes no difference
whether this modification is
carried out before or after
applying the latter.)

To test afterwards, boot the am-
ended DOS and try FORMAT d1,13.
You should see an 'Integer out
of range' report. Now try FORMAT
d1,12 and this time the command
should be accepted, giving a
disk of 240-file capacity if you
proceed with the format.


The other matter I would like to
touch on, also concerns formatt
ing. This is a trick that should
work with any DOS, provided a
DSDD drive is in use...


Although the maximum number of
tracks is officially 160 (i.e.
0-79 and 128-207), in practice
an extra track can usually be
squeezed into each side, opening
up some intriguing possibilit-
ies.To create these extra tracks
enter POKE@1,210 (or POKE@2,210
for drive 2) and format the disk
in the usual way. (Don't forget
to POKE @1/@2,208 again after-
wards, or reboot.)

The new tracks have interesting
properties that could usefully
be exploited by anyone wishing
to expand on this idea: being
isolated from and independent of
normal DOS operations, they are
unaffected by(normal) reformatt-
ing etc. and to all intents and


purposes are completely hidden
from the DOS. Any data stored
there therefore remains intact
and can only be changed through
SAVE @ (or erased by reformatt-
ing under a 210-track POKE).
Disk copying programs, including
sector copiers, also ignore the
extra tracks,making it possible,
for example, to distinguish an
original disk from a 'clone'.


However, if you do wish to copy
the new tracks from one disk to
another, use (for Betados) the
program shown on the next page
(remembering to format the
destination disk appropriately
beforehand)...



10 CLEAR 29999

20 LOAD @1,80,1,30000,10:
   REM Load track 80, disk 1

30 LOAD @1,208,1,40000,10:
   REM Load track 208, disk 1

40 SAVE @2,80,1,30000,10:
   REM Save track 80, disk 2

50 SAVE @2,208,1,40000,10:
   REM Save track 208, disk 2



Or, for G+DOS...



 10 CLEAR 29999
 20 REM Load track 80, drive 1
 30 LET a=30000: FOR s=1 TO 10
 40 LOAD @1,80,s,a
 50 LET a=a+512: REM New address
 60 NEXT s       for next sector
 70 REM Load track 208, drive 1
 80 LET a=40000: FOR s=1 TO 10
 90 LOAD @1,208,s,a
100 LET a=a+512: REM New address
110 NEXT s       for next sector
120 REM Save track 80, drive 2
130 LET a=30000: FOR s=1 TO 10
140 SAVE @2,80,s,a
150 LET a=a+512: REM New address
160 NEXT s       for next sector
170 REM Save track 208, drive 2
180 LET a=40000: FOR s=1 TO 10
190 SAVE @2,208,s,a
200 LET a=a+512: REM New address
210 NEXT s       for next sector


The new tracks are numbered 80
and 208, and can be read/written
accordingly using the LOAD @ and
SAVE @ commands. With Betados,
the multi-sector versions of
these commands have the advant-
age of conveniently allowing the
entire track to be loaded or
saved in one operation, whereas
with G+DOS each sector has to be
accessed individually.

I have tried this technique on
dozens of disks and have yet to
see it fail, although one extra
track per side does seem to be a
hard-and-fast limit. This is a
pity, as with four tracks inst-
ead of two, a means would then
exist to make a duplicate copy
of the directory -the ideal pre-
caution against a sector error.

Hopefully these ideas will offer
food for thought and stimulate
some imaginative new programming
for the Spectrum and +D.

          Best wishes,



         Miles Kinloch

Brian Cavers to Miles Kinloch

This technique even defeated a
program we use on the PC to make
duplicate disks. The program can
detect variable-format disks,
that is, disks where each track
has different numbers of sectors
and needs a special loader. But,
it disappointingly failed to
look for extra tracks!

                      Brian

 A.P.Blatherwick, WOLVERHAMPTON

I was wondering if you could do
an easy-to-use guide for Master
File using the 80-column printer
utility and the microprint faci-
lities on one of the forthcoming
disks as I find using the prog-
ram rahter complicated. Maybe a
step-by-step guide over a few
months would be an idea.

          Many thanks,

       A.P. Blatherwick

Brian Cavers to A.P. Blatherwick

I have made a  note to have a go
as soon as I can find time.

                      Brian

From: Grahame Parkyn, TRURO


Dear Ron and Brian,

On reading your editorial in
last month's OUTLET I see you
are in a quandary on how to con-
tinue with a diminishing inter-
est in all things Spectrum. Con-
sidering that the Spectrum is
now over 15 years old this state
of affairs is not surprising.

Personally I would prefer to see
OUTLET every other month than
not at all. The features which
appeal to me most of all,in ord-
er in interest are: OUTLETTERS,
DRIVECHAT, UTILITIES, OUTBOARD,
and then all the rest!


As many Spectrum enthusiasts,
myself included, now have a SAM
as well as (probably) more than
one Spectrum, might it be worth
considering including SAM items
in addition to the usual Spectr-
um items? I am not suggesting a
separate SAM edition of OUTLET,
which would probably not be
viable, but the occasional SAM
program which could be read by
SAM but not by Spectrum.

Whatever course you choose, I
will continue to support OUTLET
as long as it is available.

        Yours sincerely,

         Grahame Parkyn

Brian Cavers to Grahame Parkyn

Thanks, Grahame.

You may not be aware that we did
use to produce a SAM version of
OUTLET but it finally ended not
through lack of readership but a
lack of contributions! However,
I see no reason why any SAM pro-
grams sent in should not be put
on to the +D version of OUTLET
as an ADDENDER or similar.

                 Brian Cavers

From: L.G. Baumann, SOUTH AFRICA

Dear Mr. Cavers,

          A Suggestion
          ------------

Many people have written to you
in the past complimenting you on
Outlet and I would like to add
my voice to this. I look forward
to receiving the disc each month
and examining its contents.Thank
you for your efforts.

Here is a suggestion for Outlet:

I sense that after all this time
there is a slowing up of contri-
butions and there is now space
for the following...


Outlet has been going for 10
years and in looking back over
the earlier issues I find there
are a number of most interesting
items of which newer members
(last 5 years) are probably
unaware and which perhaps some
of the older members would also
enjoy seeing again.My suggestion
is that each month you should
choose and reproduce one item
from back issues under Addenders
or perhaps under the heading
"Looking Back"

My most-used facility is Skipper
which can jump rapidly through a
long Line being edited. It
appeared in Outlet No.53 by
Malcolm Goodman and I silently
bless him every time I use it.


I am sending you my copy as
"skipper979" but you will notice
that it is in a slightly differ-
ent form, to suit my usage.

Firstly the 979 tells me it is
in line 9979 enabling me to
check that merging it will not
interfere with an existing Line
in the programme I am working
on. Also I have transferred the
code into a string to avoid the
annoying blank screen that
always seem to follow the usual
Outlet system of using a code
line.

I do this with all the facilit-
ies taken from Outlet. It also
enables me to put into the Line
a refresher on how to use the


utility (e.g. RUN or GO SUB) and
finally I can put in a reference
to the Outlet No. in which it
appeared.

As a reminder, my disc has some
of the programs that I have sub-
mitted. They are of course the
best and used by me occasionally
otherwise I would not have
compiled them! I may of course
be biased.

Perhaps other readers could
write in about other favourites
which they have found particu-
larly useful and should be aired
again.

Although I am not a games man
there have been some very good
ones which might bear repeating.

       The 3 Wise Monkeys
       ------------------
A year ago there was a query ab-
out the 3 monkeys which Francis
Miles answered. He hoped to
track down the reason for the
sculptured relief and why monk-
eys were used as the characters.
I have been waiting now for 12
months with bated breath and am
wondering if he has been
successful.

Incidentally the pictures in the
query were displayed in the
wrong order but who cares. For
the record they should be

          Hear no evil
          Say no evil
          See no evil


It will be noted that the verbs
are in alphabetical order - a
useful mnemonic.


It so happened that our local
newspaper in a recent issue
printed the Japanese words repr-
esenting the sentences...


     Mikazaru: Hear no evil
     Mazaru:   Say no evil
     Mizaru:   See no evil


I did not know that the Japanese
language could be written in
Western alphabet. I thought that
only their own characters could
be used. Or is this a leg-pull?


          Brassed Off
          -----------
My wife and I do not go to the
pictures very often - only when
something is specially recomm-
ended by friends. We enjoyed the
film "Brassed Off", currently
showing here. Whilst knowing
what the phrase means we cannot
establish its origin. Where did
it come from? My edition of
Brewer's Dictionery of Phrase
and Fable has no entry.Does any-
one know?

           Conclusion
           ----------
Finally I would like to wish all
at Outlet and all Outlet readers
a very Happy and very Satisfact-
ory New Year for 1998.
                    L.G. Baumann.

Brian Cavers to L.G. Baumann

Yes, I use Skipper all the time
myself.

I believe the Japanese words to
be the phonetic equivalents of
the original sound of the words
in Japanese.

It's a long time since I heard
'brassed off'! Like you, I don't
know its origin. Anyone?

Incidentally, Ron managed to get
a copy of the three wise monkeys
picture you sent as a PC image
file (off the internet) though
conversion to Spectrum was very
degraded I include it here for
interest (Press GRAPHICS to see)
                     Brian.

From: Miles Kinloch, EDINBURGH

Dear Brian,

Sorry it's been so long since I've been in touch, but my spare time has been limited as I've been at college. However, here are a couple of snippets I thought may be of interest to your readers.

(From the point of view of BETAFIX, it makes no difference whether this modification is carried out before or after applying the latter.)

To test afterwards, boot the am- ended DOS and try FORMAT d1,13. You should see an 'Integer out of range' report. Now try FORMAT d1,12 and this time the command should be accepted, giving a disk of 240-file capacity if you proceed with the format.

The other matter I would like to touch on, also concerns formatt ing. This is a trick that should work with any DOS, provided a DSDD drive is in use...

Although the maximum number of tracks is officially 160 (i.e. 0-79 and 128-207), in practice an extra track can usually be squeezed into each side, opening up some intriguing possibilit- ies.To create these extra tracks enter POKE@1,210 (or POKE@2,210 for drive 2) and format the disk in the usual way. (Don't forget to POKE @1/@2,208 again after- wards, or reboot.)

The new tracks have interesting properties that could usefully be exploited by anyone wishing to expand on this idea: being isolated from and independent of normal DOS operations, they are unaffected by(normal) reformatt- ing etc. and to all intents and

purposes are completely hidden from the DOS. Any data stored there therefore remains intact and can only be changed through SAVE @ (or erased by reformatt- ing under a 210-track POKE). Disk copying programs, including sector copiers, also ignore the extra tracks,making it possible, for example, to distinguish an original disk from a 'clone'.

However, if you do wish to copy the new tracks from one disk to another, use (for Betados) the program shown on the next page (remembering to format the destination disk appropriately beforehand)...

10 CLEAR 29999

```text
20 LOAD @1,80,1,30000,10:
```

REM Load track 80, disk 1

```text
30 LOAD @1,208,1,40000,10:
```

REM Load track 208, disk 1

```text
40 SAVE @2,80,1,30000,10:
```

REM Save track 80, disk 2

```text
50 SAVE @2,208,1,40000,10:
```

REM Save track 208, disk 2

Or, for G+DOS...

10 CLEAR 29999 20 REM Load track 80, drive 1 30 LET a=30000: FOR s=1 TO 10 40 LOAD @1,80,s,a 50 LET a=a+512: REM New address 60 NEXT s       for next sector 70 REM Load track 208, drive 1 80 LET a=40000: FOR s=1 TO 10 90 LOAD @1,208,s,a 100 LET a=a+512: REM New address 110 NEXT s       for next sector 120 REM Save track 80, drive 2 130 LET a=30000: FOR s=1 TO 10 140 SAVE @2,80,s,a 150 LET a=a+512: REM New address 160 NEXT s       for next sector 170 REM Save track 208, drive 2 180 LET a=40000: FOR s=1 TO 10 190 SAVE @2,208,s,a 200 LET a=a+512: REM New address 210 NEXT s       for next sector

The new tracks are numbered 80 and 208, and can be read/written accordingly using the LOAD @ and SAVE @ commands. With Betados, the multi-sector versions of these commands have the advant- age of conveniently allowing the entire track to be loaded or saved in one operation, whereas with G+DOS each sector has to be accessed individually.

I have tried this technique on dozens of disks and have yet to see it fail, although one extra track per side does seem to be a hard-and-fast limit. This is a pity, as with four tracks inst- ead of two, a means would then exist to make a duplicate copy of the directory -the ideal pre- caution against a sector error.

Hopefully these ideas will offer food for thought and stimulate some imaginative new programming for the Spectrum and +D.

Best wishes,

Miles Kinloch

Brian Cavers to Miles Kinloch

This technique even defeated a program we use on the PC to make duplicate disks. The program can detect variable-format disks, that is, disks where each track has different numbers of sectors and needs a special loader. But, it disappointingly failed to look for extra tracks!

Brian

**От:** Miles Kinloch, EDINBURGH

Дорогой Brian,

Прошу прощения, что так долго не выходил на связь: свободного времени было в обрез из-за учебы в колледже. Тем не менее, вот пара заметок, которые, как мне кажется, могут заинтересовать ваших читателей.

Экспериментируя недавно с возможностью Betados создавать расширенные форматы каталога, я обнаружил, что если заданная емкость превышает 255 файлов, начинаются сбои: это бьет по выводу оглавления и адресации файлов.

Я выяснил причину: DOS использует однобайтовую системную переменную (по адресу 15874) для номера слота каталога. Хотя для формата на 80 файлов, под который она и проектировалась, этого хватало, максимально возможное значение здесь — всего 255. Поскольку замена системной переменной на двухбайтовую потребовала бы масштабной переделки DOS, а практический предел в 240 файлов (ближайшее значение, соответствующее полному набору дорожек каталога) все равно дает солидную емкость, проще всего смириться с этими ограничениями и пропатчить (POKE) DOS, сузив диапазон параметра FORMAT.

Напомню, максимальное число дорожек каталога в настоящее время равно 39, что соответствует 780 файлам. Диск форматируется командой `FORMAT d1,n`, где `n` — число дорожек каталога (в данном случае 39). При любом большем значении возникнет ошибка «Integer out of range». Чтобы установить максимальный предел в 240 файлов, нам нужно уменьшить наибольшее допустимое значение `n` до 12. Это можно сделать, изменив DOS следующим образом:

```text
10 CLEAR 4e4
20 LOAD d1"+sys Beta"CODE 40960
30 POKE 46415,9
40 SAVE d1"+sys Beta"CODE 40960,6850
```

(С точки зрения BETAFIX нет никакой разницы, вносить это исправление до или после ее применения.)

Для проверки загрузите измененную DOS и попробуйте ввести `FORMAT d1,13`. Должно появиться сообщение «Integer out of range». Теперь попробуйте `FORMAT d1,12` — на этот раз команда должна быть принята, и при продолжении форматирования вы получите диск емкостью 240 файлов.

Другой вопрос, которого я хотел бы коснуться, тоже относится к форматированию. Этот трюк должен работать с любой DOS при условии, что используется дисковод DSDD...

Хотя максимальное количество дорожек официально равно 160 (то есть 0-79 и 128-207), на практике с каждой стороны обычно можно выжать еще по одной дорожке, что открывает интригующие возможности. Чтобы создать эти дополнительные дорожки, введите `POKE @1,210` (или `POKE @2,210` для дисковода 2) и отформатируйте диск обычным способом. (Не забудьте потом снова вернуть `POKE @1/@2,208` или перезагрузиться.)

Новые дорожки обладают интересными свойствами, которые пригодятся любому, кто захочет развить эту идею: будучи изолированными и независимыми от обычных дисковых операций DOS, они не страдают при (обычном) переформатировании и фактически полностью скрыты от DOS. Любые записанные туда данные остаются в неприкосновенности и могут быть изменены только через `SAVE @` (или стерты переформатированием после POKE на 210 дорожек). Программы копирования дисков, включая посекторные копировщики, также игнорируют эти дорожки, что позволяет, например, отличать оригинальный диск от клона.

Однако, если вы хотите скопировать эти нестандартные дорожки с одного диска на другой, используйте (для Betados) программу ниже (не забыв заранее соответствующим образом отформатировать целевой диск)...

```text
10 CLEAR 29999
20 LOAD @1,80,1,30000,10: REM Load track 80, disk 1
30 LOAD @1,208,1,40000,10: REM Load track 208, disk 1
40 SAVE @2,80,1,30000,10: REM Save track 80, disk 2
50 SAVE @2,208,1,40000,10: REM Save track 208, disk 2
```

Или для G+DOS...

```text
 10 CLEAR 29999
 20 REM Load track 80, drive 1
 30 LET a=30000: FOR s=1 TO 10
 40 LOAD @1,80,s,a
 50 LET a=a+512: REM New address
 60 NEXT s       for next sector
 70 REM Load track 208, drive 1
 80 LET a=40000: FOR s=1 TO 10
 90 LOAD @1,208,s,a
100 LET a=a+512: REM New address
110 NEXT s       for next sector
120 REM Save track 80, drive 2
130 LET a=30000: FOR s=1 TO 10
140 SAVE @2,80,s,a
150 LET a=a+512: REM New address
160 NEXT s       for next sector
170 REM Save track 208, drive 2
180 LET a=40000: FOR s=1 TO 10
190 SAVE @2,208,s,a
200 LET a=a+512: REM New address
210 NEXT s       for next sector
```

Новые дорожки имеют номера 80 и 208, и к ним можно обращаться для чтения и записи соответственно с помощью команд LOAD @ и SAVE @. В Betados многосекторные версии этих команд дают преимущество, позволяя удобно загружать или сохранять всю дорожку за одну операцию, тогда как в G+DOS к каждому сектору приходится обращаться отдельно.

Я опробовал эту методику на десятках дискет и пока ни разу не видел сбоев, хотя одна дополнительная дорожка на сторону, похоже, является жестким пределом. Жаль, ведь имей мы четыре дорожки вместо двух, появился бы способ сделать дубликат каталога — идеальная страховка от секторных ошибок.

Надеюсь, эти идеи дадут пищу для размышлений и вдохновят на создание новых оригинальных программ для Spectrum и +D.

С наилучшими пожеланиями,  
Miles Kinloch

### Предложение

Многие читатели писали вам в прошлом, выражая восхищение журналом Outlet, и я хотел бы присоединиться к ним. Я каждый месяц с нетерпением жду диск и изучаю его содержимое. Спасибо за ваш труд.

Вот предложение для Outlet:

Я чувствую, что спустя столько времени поток присылаемых материалов ослабевает, и теперь появилось место для следующего...

Outlet выходит уже 10 лет, и, оглядываясь на ранние выпуски, я нахожу там множество интереснейших вещей, о которых новые подписчики (за последние 5 лет), вероятно, и не знают, а старым читателям, возможно, было бы приятно увидеть их снова. Мое предложение состоит в том, чтобы каждый месяц выбирать и перепечатывать один материал из старых номеров в разделе Addenders или, возможно, под заголовком «Взгляд в прошлое» (Looking Back).

Моя самая используемая утилита — Skipper, которая позволяет быстро перемещаться по длинной редактируемой строке. Она появилась в Outlet №53 за авторством Malcolm Goodman, и я мысленно благодарю его каждый раз, когда ею пользуюсь.

Я высылаю вам свою копию под именем «skipper979», но вы заметите, что она в немного измененном виде, адаптированном под мои нужды.

Во-первых, число 979 говорит мне о том, что она находится в строке 9979, позволяя заранее проверить, не затрет ли объединение (MERGE) существующую строку в программе, над которой я работаю. Кроме того, я перенес машинный код в строковую переменную, чтобы избежать раздражающего пустого экрана, который неизменно появляется при обычном для Outlet способе хранения кода в строке программы.

### Три мудрые обезьяны

Год назад был вопрос о трех обезьянах, на который ответил Francis Miles. Он надеялся выяснить причину появления этого скульптурного рельефа и то, почему именно обезьяны были выбраны в качестве персонажей. Я ждал 12 месяцев затаив дыхание и теперь гадаю, увенчались ли его поиски успехом.

Кстати, картинки в том вопросе были показаны в неправильном порядке, но кого это волнует. Для протокола, порядок должен быть таким:

```text
          Hear no evil  (Не слышу зла)
          Say no evil   (Не говорю о зле)
          See no evil   (Не вижу зла)
```

Заметьте, что глаголы идут в алфавитном порядке (в английском языке: Hear, Say, See) — полезная мнемоника.

Так совпало, что наша местная газета в недавнем выпуске напечатала японские слова, обозначающие эти фразы...

```text
     Mikazaru: Hear no evil
     Mazaru:   Say no evil
     Mizaru:   See no evil
```

Я и не знал, что японский язык можно записывать западным алфавитом. Я думал, что можно использовать только их собственные иероглифы. Или это розыгрыш?
